paragraphs.heading: Everyday optical tools
paragraphs.text: Optics is the branch of physics that studies light and other electromagnetic radiation, including how it meets matter and the instruments that use or detect it. Mirrors and lenses are among its practical uses, as are telescopes, microscopes, lasers and fibre optics. These show up in a range of technologies and in everyday objects.

paragraphs.heading: Thinking in rays
paragraphs.text: Practical optics usually relies on simplified models, and the most common is geometric optics. It treats light as a set of rays that move in straight lines and bend when they pass through a surface or reflect from it. Wave effects such as diffraction and interference fall outside this model and need a fuller one, physical optics.

paragraphs.heading: The first lenses
paragraphs.text: Optics began with lenses made by the ancient Egyptians and Mesopotamians. The earliest known ones were polished crystal, often quartz, from Crete, dating from as early as 2000 BC. Lenses from Rhodes date to around 700 BC, as do Assyrian ones such as the Nimrud lens. The ancient Greeks and Romans made lenses by filling glass spheres with water.

paragraphs.heading: Early thinking about mirrors
paragraphs.text: Plato commented on the parity reversal of mirrors in his Timaeus. Euclid stated that light follows the shortest path and studied multiple reflections in flat and spherical mirrors. Later, Plutarch described multiple reflections in spherical mirrors and discussed images that are magnified or reduced, both real and imaginary.

paragraphs.heading: Refraction and shape
paragraphs.text: Ptolemy described a way to measure the angle of refraction, but he missed how it relates to the angle of incidence. In 984, the Persian mathematician Ibn Sahl wrote a treatise titled On burning mirrors and lenses. In it he correctly set out a law of refraction equivalent to Snell's law. He then used that law to work out the best shapes for lenses and curved mirrors.

paragraphs.heading: Glass that magnifies
paragraphs.text: In the early 11th century, Alhazen explored reflection and refraction in his Book of Optics, building on observation and experiment. Roger Bacon used parts of glass spheres as magnifying glasses. With them he showed that light reflects from objects rather than being sent out from them.
